chapter_note.about: A hypothesis test asks whether the data are too surprising to blame on chance if a default claim (the null) were true. You set up H0 and H1, standardise the sample statistic, and compare it with a cut-off from a table or turn it into a p-value. The test can go wrong in two ways, which are Type I and Type II errors, and the chapter covers the z, t and chi-square versions, with confidence intervals as the matching view. The marks table shows no past-paper questions tagged to this chapter yet, so the patterns below come from the ladder and from how these tests are usually asked.
chapter_note.simple: A test starts by assuming the boring claim is true, like 'this coin is fair', and then asks whether your data are so unusual under that claim that you stop believing it. You measure how far your result is from the claim in units of typical wobble, and compare it to a cut-off chosen in advance. Two mistakes are possible: crying wolf when the claim was fine, or missing a real problem. Making one rarer makes the other more common unless you collect more data. Different tests suit different data: averages (z or t), shares (z), counts in categories (chi-square), and spread (chi-square). A range you compute for the true value is the same test seen from the other side. In exam words: H0 and H1, test statistic, critical value or p-value, Type I and II errors, z, t and chi-square tests, and duality with confidence intervals.

cards.title: Null and alternative hypotheses
cards.simple: A phone maker says its battery lasts at least 10 hours. A reviewer thinks it is shorter. In a test, we assume the maker is right until the data make that hard to believe, like a court that assumes someone is innocent until the evidence is strong. The 'assume innocent' statement is the null hypothesis, and it always uses an equals sign: the average is exactly 10. The reviewer's suspicion is the alternative: the average is less than 10. The words in the suspicion tell you which side to look at: 'less' means look at the low end, 'more' the high end, 'different' both ends. In exam words: H0 holds the equality, H1 holds the claim to be shown, and its direction sets a one-sided or two-sided test.
cards.idea: A hypothesis test starts by assuming a default, the **null hypothesis H0**, which always contains an equals sign. The suspicion or claim you want evidence for is the **alternative H1**. Its direction decides where you look: one side for 'less' or 'more', both sides for 'different'.
cards.definition:
$H_0:\mu=\mu_0$ against one of:

- $H_1:\mu<\mu_0$ (left-tailed),
- $H_1:\mu>\mu_0$ (right-tailed),
- $H_1:\mu\ne\mu_0$ (two-tailed).

The data are used to decide whether to **reject H0** or to **fail to reject H0**. Never say 'accept H0': keeping H0 only means the evidence was not strong enough.

Symbols: μ is the unknown population mean and μ0 is the value claimed in H0.
cards.intuition_full: The test is built to control one kind of mistake: rejecting H0 when it is true. To control that, H0 must be a single precise value, so we can work out how the statistic behaves if H0 is true. That is why H0 has the equals sign, even if the original claim is 'at least 10', because the boundary value 10 is the hardest case for H0. The alternative is the statement you are trying to find evidence for, so it goes in H1. A researcher who wants to prove that a new method is better puts 'better' in H1. The direction of H1 decides the rejection region: for 'less than', only very low sample means count as evidence, so the region is the left tail.

example.setup: A tablet maker claims the battery lasts at least 10 hours. A reviewer suspects it lasts less. Set up H0 and H1 and say where the rejection region lies.
steps: The claim is 'at least 10 hours'. The reviewer's suspicion is 'less than 10 hours'.
H0 holds the equality at the boundary: H0: μ = 10.
H1 holds the suspicion: H1: μ < 10.
'Less than' points to the low side, so this is a left-tailed test.
Decision rule: reject H0 only if the sample mean is far enough below 10.
example.answer: H0: μ = 10, H1: μ < 10, left-tailed. Reject if x-bar is very low.

steps: The researcher wants to find evidence for 'above 60'. That claim goes in H1.
So H1: μ > 60, a right-tailed test.
H0 must hold the equality: H0: μ = 60.
Option (a) puts the suspicion in H0 and the equality in H1. It is wrong on both counts.
The answer is (b).

cards.title: z statistic and critical value
cards.simple: You want to know if your sample average is far from the claimed average. 'Far' means in units of the typical wobble of an average, the standard error. So take the gap between your average and the claimed one and divide by the wobble. That count is the z statistic. Then you need a line in the sand. Before the test, you pick how rarely you are willing to be fooled, usually 5%, and that gives a cut-off value from the table, 1.645 for one side. If your count is beyond the cut-off, the result is too unusual to blame on luck, so you reject the claim. In exam words: z = (x-bar - μ0)/(σ/√n), and reject H0 if z is beyond the critical value.
cards.idea: The **z statistic** measures how many standard errors the sample mean lies from the value claimed in H0. The **critical value** is the cut-off, set by the significance level α. If the statistic lands beyond the cut-off, in the rejection region, you reject H0.
cards.definition:
$$z=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}$$

Reject H0 when z is beyond the critical value: right-tailed $z>z_\alpha$, left-tailed $z<-z_\alpha$, two-tailed $|z|>z_{\alpha/2}$.

Critical values: one-sided at 5% is 1.645 and at 1% is 2.326; two-sided at 5% is 1.96 and at 1% is 2.576.

Symbols: σ is the known population SD, n the sample size, α the significance level.
cards.intuition_full: If H0 is true, X-bar is approximately N(μ0, σ^2/n), so z is N(0, 1). The rejection region is chosen so that, when H0 is true, z lands in it with probability exactly α. That is why α is the chance of a false alarm. Values of z near 0 are what H0 predicts, and values far out are rare under H0, so they count as evidence against it. The division by σ/√n is crucial: it converts the raw gap in the original units into standard errors. A gap of 2.8 can be huge or tiny depending on the standard error. For a one-sided test all the probability α is in one tail, which is why the cut-off 1.645 is smaller than the two-sided 1.96.

example.setup: H0: μ = 80 against H1: μ > 80. A sample of n = 49 has x-bar = 83.5 and σ = 10 is known. Test at 5% (critical value 1.645). Then repeat with x-bar = 81.7.
steps: Standard error = σ / sqrt(n) = 10 / 7 = 1.4286.
Right-tailed at 5%: the critical value is 1.645.
2.45 is beyond 1.645, so z falls in the rejection region: reject H0.
With x-bar = 81.7: z = 1.7 / 1.4286 = 1.19, which is below 1.645. Fail to reject H0.
example.answer: z = 2.45 > 1.645, reject H0. With x-bar = 81.7, z = 1.19, fail to reject.

examples.setup: H0: μ = 100 against H1: μ ≠ 100, σ = 15, n = 36, x-bar = 94.5. Decide at 5% (critical 1.96) and at 1% (critical 2.576).
steps: Standard error = 15 / 6 = 2.5.
Two-tailed: compare |z| = 2.2 with the critical value.
At 5%: 2.2 > 1.96, so reject H0.
At 1%: 2.2 < 2.576, so fail to reject H0. The decision depends on α.

examples.setup: The same data as the first example: n = 49, σ = 10, x-bar = 83.5, H0: μ = 80. A student divides by σ instead of σ / sqrt(n). What do they conclude?
steps: Student's statistic: (83.5 - 80) / 10 = 0.35.
That is far below 1.645, so the student fails to reject H0.
The correct statistic is 3.5 / 1.4286 = 2.45, which rejects H0.
The student's error turned a clear result into no result.
Always divide by the standard error σ / sqrt(n), not by σ.
examples.answer: The student wrongly fails to reject. The correct z = 2.45 rejects H0.

cards.why: This is the core mechanical step of a z-test: standardise and compare. In GATE: compute z from the summary data, or decide reject versus keep using a given critical value.
how: Write μ0, σ, n and x-bar.
Standard error = σ / sqrt(n).
z = (x-bar - μ0) / SE.
Pick the critical value from the tail of H1 and the level α.
Reject H0 if z is in the rejection region, otherwise fail to reject.
cards.mistake: Dividing by σ instead of σ / √n, or using the two-sided critical value for a one-sided test. A second slip is comparing z with the critical value on the wrong side: for a left-tailed test the rejection region is z below -1.645.
edge_cases: Left-tailed: reject if z < -z_α. Check the sign of z.
The boundary case z equal to the critical value: it rejects at exactly that α in most textbooks, but such ties are unlikely in questions.
Changing α changes the decision: 2.2 rejects at 5% but not at 1%.
σ must be known. If it is not, use s and the t distribution.
connections: The p-value is the same comparison turned around (next card).
With σ unknown, z becomes t (t-test card).
The rejection region probability is the Type I error (error card).

cards.title: p-value
cards.simple: Suppose a friend says a coin is fair and you toss it 100 times and get 63 heads. Ask: if the coin really were fair, how often would I see something at least this far from 50? If that chance is tiny, like 1%, either you saw a rare fluke or the coin is not fair. That chance is the p-value. A small p-value means the data would be surprising if the claim were true. We compare it to a line drawn in advance, such as 5%: below the line, we stop believing the claim. A common wrong reading is that the p-value is the chance the claim is true. It is not. It is the chance of data this extreme if the claim is true. In exam words: p = P(data this extreme | H0), reject H0 if p < α, and double the tail for a two-sided test.
cards.idea: The **p-value** is the probability, if H0 is true, of getting a result at least as extreme as the one you observed. Small means the data are surprising under H0. You **reject H0 if p is less than α**. For a two-sided test, count both tails, so double the one-tail area.
cards.definition:
For a z-test with observed statistic $z_{obs}$:

- right-tailed: $p=1-\Phi(z_{obs})$,
- left-tailed: $p=\Phi(z_{obs})$,
- two-tailed: $p=2\,(1-\Phi(|z_{obs}|))$.

Decision: reject H0 when $p<\alpha$.

The p-value is **not** $P(H_0\text{ is true})$ and not the probability of a Type I error for this one result.
cards.intuition_full: The p-value turns the critical-value comparison inside out. Instead of fixing α and finding the cut-off, you take your statistic as the cut-off and ask how much probability lies beyond it under H0. Comparing p with α gives exactly the same decision as comparing z with the critical value, since p < α holds exactly when z is beyond the cut-off. The advantage is that p tells you how strong the evidence is, not just whether it passes one line. The probability lives in the world where H0 is true, so it cannot tell you the chance that H0 is true. That would need a prior, as in Bayes' rule. For a two-sided alternative, an extreme result in either direction counts as evidence, so you add both tails.

example.setup: A z-test gives z = 1.7. Given Φ(1.7) = 0.9554, find the p-value for a right-tailed test and for a two-tailed test, and decide at α = 0.05.
steps: The observed statistic is z = 1.7.
Right-tailed p-value = 1 - Φ(1.7) = 1 - 0.9554 = 0.0446.
0.0446 < 0.05, so the right-tailed test rejects H0.
Two-tailed: double the tail, p = 2 x 0.0446 = 0.0892.
0.0892 > 0.05, so the two-tailed test fails to reject H0.
example.answer: Right-tailed p = 0.0446 (reject). Two-tailed p = 0.0892 (fail to reject).

At α = 0.01: p = 0.03 > 0.01, so fail to reject H0.
Meaning: if H0 were true, there would be a 3% chance of data at least this extreme.
It does not mean P(H0 is true) = 0.03.
It also does not mean there is a 97% chance that H1 is true.
examples.answer: Reject at 5%, fail to reject at 1%. The p-value is P(data this extreme | H0), not P(H0).

examples.setup: A left-tailed z-test gives z = -2.3. Given Φ(2.3) = 0.9893, find the p-value and decide at 5% and 1%.
steps: At 1%: 0.0107 > 0.01, fail to reject H0.
The result sits just on the wrong side of 1%. Close to the line, the decision is fragile.
Do not double the tail here: the alternative is one-sided.
examples.answer: p = 0.0107: reject at 5%, fail to reject at 1%.

cards.why: The p-value is how real results are reported, and it is the most misread quantity in statistics. In GATE: compute a p-value from z, convert between one-sided and two-sided, or choose the correct meaning of a p-value from a list.
how: Compute the test statistic z.
Find the tail area beyond z in the direction of H1.
For a two-tailed test, double it.
Compare p with α: reject if p < α.
If asked for the meaning, say: probability of data at least this extreme if H0 is true.
cards.mistake: Reading the p-value as the probability that H0 is true. A second slip is forgetting to double the tail for a two-sided test, which halves the p-value and can flip the decision.
edge_cases: Large p does not prove H0: it only means you lack evidence against it.
Same z, different tails: the two-tailed p is twice the one-tailed p.
p and the critical value give the same decision for the same α.
A very small p does not mean a large effect: with a huge n even tiny differences give small p.
connections: The same decision as the critical value in the z statistic card.
The Bayes posterior P(H0 | data) is a different quantity and needs a prior (prob.bayes).
p-values and confidence intervals tell the same story (duality card).

**Worked example.** A z-test gives z = 1.7. Given Φ(1.7) = 0.9554, find the p-value for a right-tailed test and for a two-tailed test, and decide at α = 0.05.

1. The observed statistic is z = 1.7.
2. Right-tailed p-value = 1 - Φ(1.7) = 1 - 0.9554 = 0.0446.
3. 0.0446 < 0.05, so the right-tailed test rejects H0.
4. Two-tailed: double the tail, p = 2 x 0.0446 = 0.0892.
5. 0.0892 > 0.05, so the two-tailed test fails to reject H0.

**Answer:** Right-tailed p = 0.0446 (reject). Two-tailed p = 0.0892 (fail to reject).

**Check yourself:** A right-tailed test has z = 2.0 and Φ(2.0) = 0.9772. Find the p-value.

cards.title: Type I error, Type II error, power and trade-offs
cards.simple: Think of a smoke alarm. It can ring when there is no fire (a false alarm) or stay silent when there is a fire (a miss). A test also makes two kinds of mistakes. Rejecting a claim that is actually true is the false alarm, and its chance is alpha, which you choose. Failing to reject a claim that is actually false is the miss, and its chance is beta. Power is the chance of catching a real problem, 1 minus beta. Here is the catch: if you make the alarm less jumpy so it rarely gives false alarms, it misses more real fires. The only way to improve both is a better detector, which in testing means a bigger sample. In exam words: alpha = P(reject | H0 true), beta = P(keep | H1 true), power = 1 - beta; for a fixed n, lowering alpha raises beta.
cards.idea: A test can go wrong in two ways. A **Type I error** rejects H0 when it is true, with probability **α**. A **Type II error** keeps H0 when it is false, with probability **β**. The **power** 1 - β is the chance of catching a real effect. For a fixed sample size, lowering α raises β. A larger sample, or a larger true effect, raises power.
cards.definition:
$$\alpha=P(\text{reject }H_0\mid H_0\text{ true}),\qquad \beta=P(\text{keep }H_0\mid H_1\text{ true}),\qquad \text{power}=1-\beta$$

To compute β or power you need a specific true value of μ. Find the cut-off for x-bar from H0, then find the probability of falling on the keep side (for β) or the reject side (for power) when μ takes the true value.

Symbols: α is the significance level you choose, and β depends on the true μ, σ and n.
cards.intuition_full: Picture two bell curves for the statistic, one centred where H0 says and one where the truth lies. The cut-off line splits the plane. The part of the H0 curve beyond the line is α: rejections that should not have happened. The part of the true curve on the other side is β: failures to reject that should have happened. Moving the line to the right shrinks α but grows β, and that is the whole trade-off. The only way to shrink both is to pull the curves apart or make them narrower. A bigger sample makes each curve narrower (SE shrinks) and also moves the two curves further apart in standard errors. A bigger true difference also separates them.

example.setup: A right-tailed z-test of H0 against a true alternative that lies 2 standard errors above H0. Find α and β for cutoffs 1.645 and 2.33, and the power when the sample is larger and the alternative lies 3.3 standard errors above H0. Given Φ(-0.355) = 0.3613, Φ(0.33) = 0.6293, Φ(-1.655) = 0.049.
steps: Two worlds: the H0 curve is centred at 0 and the H1 curve at 2, in standard-error units. Reject H0 to the right of a cutoff.
Cutoff 2.33: α = 0.01 and β = Φ(2.33 - 2) = Φ(0.33) = 0.629. Lowering α raised β.
A larger sample moves the H1 curve to 3.3 (in standard errors). With cutoff 1.645, β = Φ(1.645 - 3.3) = Φ(-1.655) = 0.049.
example.answer: At cutoff 1.645: α = 5%, β = 36%. At 2.33: α = 1%, β = 63%. With the larger sample: β = 5%, power = 95%.

cards.title: t-test for a mean
cards.simple: Sometimes you do not know how spread out the population is, so you use the spread of your own small sample as a stand-in. That stand-in is itself uncertain, so we compare against a slightly fatter bell curve, the t curve, which makes us a bit more careful. Everything else is the same as before: divide the gap between your average and the claim by the wobble of an average, which is the sample spread divided by the square root of n. Then check it against the t table row for n minus 1. With few data points, the cut-off is bigger, so you need a bigger gap before you reject. In exam words: t = (x-bar - μ0)/(s/√n) with n - 1 degrees of freedom.
cards.idea: When σ is unknown, replace it with the sample SD s. The statistic **t = (x-bar - μ0)/(s/√n)** follows a **t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom** if the data are normal. The t table's cut-offs are larger than z's, so the test is more cautious for small samples.
cards.definition:
$$t=\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt n},\qquad \text{df}=n-1,\qquad s^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum(x_i-\bar x)^2$$

Reject H0 when t is beyond the critical value $t_{\alpha,\,n-1}$ (one-sided) or $t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ (two-sided).

Symbols: s is the sample SD with divisor n - 1, and n - 1 is the degrees of freedom. As n grows, t critical values approach z.
cards.intuition_full: The z statistic needs σ, but we only have s, which varies from sample to sample. The ratio of a normal to an estimated scale has heavier tails than the normal, and this is exactly the t distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom. Heavier tails mean larger critical values. For 8 degrees of freedom the two-sided 5% cut-off is 2.306, compared with 1.96 for z. As the sample gets bigger, s becomes a reliable stand-in for σ, and the cut-off approaches 1.96. Degrees of freedom = n - 1 = 8. Two-sided 5%: critical value 2.306.
|t| = 2.0 < 2.306, so the two-sided test fails to reject H0.
Right-tailed 5%: critical value 1.860. Since 2.0 > 1.860, the one-sided test rejects H0.
example.answer: t = 2.0 with 8 df. Two-sided: fail to reject. Right-tailed: reject.

cards.title: z-test for a proportion
cards.simple: You think a coin is fair, but it shows 118 heads in 200 tosses. Is that too many to blame on luck? First, 118 out of 200 is 59%. If the coin is fair, the number of heads wobbles around 50% by a typical amount that depends on how many tosses you did. That wobble is the square root of (half times half) over 200. Count how many wobbles away 59% is from 50%, and compare with the cut-off 1.96. The wobble uses the claimed 50%, not your 59%, because you are testing the claim. In exam words: z = (p-hat - p0)/√(p0(1 - p0)/n), using p0 in the standard error.
cards.idea: To test a claimed proportion p0, compute the sample proportion p-hat and measure its gap from p0 in standard errors. The standard error is built from **p0**, not from p-hat, because H0 is assumed true. The normal approximation needs enough data: np0 and n(1 - p0) both at least about 10.
cards.definition:
$$z=\frac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}},\qquad \hat p=\frac xn$$

Use the same critical values or p-values as the z-test for a mean.

Condition: $np_0\ge10$ and $n(1-p_0)\ge10$.

Symbols: x is the number of successes, n the sample size, p0 the value in H0.
cards.intuition_full: A count of successes is binomial, so p-hat has mean p0 and variance p0(1 - p0)/n if H0 is true. By the CLT, p-hat is approximately normal, so z is approximately standard normal. The variance depends on p, and in a test we use the value claimed by H0, because we want to know how p-hat behaves in the world where H0 holds. A confidence interval is different: there p is unknown, so p-hat goes into the standard error. The normal approximation needs both expected counts np0 and n(1 - p0) to be reasonably large. For rare events, with np0 small, the binomial is skewed and the normal curve is not a good fit, so use an exact binomial test instead.

example.setup: H0: p = 0.5 against H1: p ≠ 0.5. In n = 200 tosses there are 118 heads. Test at 5% (critical 1.96).

|z| = 2.55 > 1.96, so reject H0 at 5%. The coin looks biased.
Note: using p-hat in the SE would give sqrt(0.59 x 0.41 / 200) = 0.0348 and z = 2.59, slightly different. The test uses p0.

cards.title: Chi-square goodness of fit
cards.simple: You claim a bag has red, blue and green sweets in the ratio 2 : 1 : 1. You take out 120 and count them. If the claim is true, you would expect 60 red, 30 blue and 30 green. Real counts will not match exactly, so measure how far off they are. For each colour take the gap between what you saw and what you expected, square it, and divide by what you expected. Add them up. If the total is small, your counts are close to the claim. If it is large, the claim looks wrong. To judge 'large', compare with the chi-square table. In exam words: chi-square = the sum of (O - E)^2 / E, with k - 1 degrees of freedom.
cards.idea: A **goodness-of-fit** test asks whether observed counts match a claimed set of probabilities. For each category compute (observed - expected)^2 / expected and add them up. A small total means a good fit. Compare with the chi-square cut-off at k - 1 degrees of freedom, minus one more for every parameter estimated from the data.
cards.definition:
$$\chi^2=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{(O_i-E_i)^2}{E_i},\qquad E_i=n\,p_i,\qquad \text{df}=k-1-m$$

Reject H0 when chi-square exceeds the right-tail critical value. Rule of thumb: every expected count should be at least 5.

Symbols: O_i is the observed count, E_i the expected count under H0, k the number of categories, and m the number of parameters estimated from the data.
cards.intuition_full: Each term (O - E)^2 / E measures one category's gap, squared so that above and below both count, and scaled by E so that a gap of 8 matters more when only 30 are expected than when 600 are. Under H0 each term is roughly a squared standard normal, so the sum behaves like a chi-square variable. The degrees of freedom are fewer than k because the observed counts must add to n, which means once k - 1 are known the last is fixed. Each parameter estimated from the data removes another degree of freedom, since the fit then uses the data to match the model. A chi-square test is always right-tailed: only large totals are evidence against H0.

steps: Expected counts: red 120 x 1/2 = 60, blue 120 x 1/4 = 30, green 30.
Degrees of freedom = k - 1 = 2, critical value 5.991.
3.2 < 5.991, so fail to reject H0. The counts are consistent with 2 : 1 : 1.
example.answer: Chi-square = 3.2 with 2 df, fail to reject.

cards.title: Chi-square test of independence
cards.simple: You give two treatments to 120 patients and record whether they got better, stayed the same or got worse. Does the treatment matter? If it did not, then both groups would have the same mix of outcomes. So work out what each box in the table would hold if treatment and outcome were unrelated: for each box, multiply its row total by its column total and divide by everyone. Then compare the real counts with these 'unrelated' counts using the same chi-square sum as before. A big total means the treatment and outcome are linked. In exam words: E = row total x column total / N, chi-square = sum of (O - E)^2 / E, df = (r - 1)(c - 1).
cards.idea: A **test of independence** asks whether two categorical variables in a table are related. If they were independent, each cell's expected count would be its row total times its column total divided by N. Add up (O - E)^2 / E over all cells and compare with chi-square at (r - 1)(c - 1) degrees of freedom.
cards.definition:
$$E_{ij}=\frac{R_i\,C_j}{N},\qquad \chi^2=\sum_{i,j}\frac{(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2}{E_{ij}},\qquad \text{df}=(r-1)(c-1)$$

Symbols: R_i is the total of row i, C_j the total of column j, N the grand total, r and c the numbers of rows and columns.

For a 2 x 2 table [[a, b], [c, d]] there is a shortcut: $\chi^2=\dfrac{N(ad-bc)^2}{R_1R_2C_1C_2}$.
cards.intuition_full: If the variables are independent, the chance of falling in cell (i, j) is the product of the row share and the column share. Multiplying by N gives R_i C_j / N, which is the expected count. The marginal totals are used up in this calculation, so the cells are not free: once the row and column totals are fixed, only (r - 1)(c - 1) cells can vary. That is the degrees of freedom. The test statistic is the same sum as in goodness of fit, because it again compares observed with expected counts. The 2 x 2 shortcut comes from algebra on that sum and is quicker: all four terms are equal up to a sign and simplify to one fraction.

df = (2 - 1)(3 - 1) = 2, critical value 5.991. Since 14.91 > 5.991, reject independence: treatment and outcome are related.

cards.title: Chi-square test for a variance
cards.simple: A machine is supposed to make parts with a spread (variance) of 9. You measure 16 parts and find their sample variance is 18, twice as large. Is that too much to blame on luck? A sample variance wobbles, so you need a yardstick. Multiply the sample variance by (n minus 1) and divide by the claimed variance. If the claim is true, that number follows a chi-square curve with n minus 1 degrees of freedom. Here that number is 15 times 18 divided by 9, which is 30. The chi-square table says 25 is the 5% line for 15 degrees of freedom, so 30 is too big to be luck, and we reject the claim. In exam words: chi-square = (n - 1)s^2/σ0^2 with n - 1 degrees of freedom, and the test is usually one-sided.
cards.idea: To test a claim about the **variance** of a normal population, scale the sample variance by (n - 1) and divide by the claimed variance. If H0 is true, the result follows a **chi-square distribution with n - 1 degrees of freedom**. A large value points to a bigger variance and a small value to a smaller one.
cards.definition:
$$\chi^2=\frac{(n-1)\,s^2}{\sigma_0^2}\sim\chi^2_{n-1}\quad\text{under }H_0:\sigma^2=\sigma_0^2$$

Right-tailed ($H_1:\sigma^2>\sigma_0^2$): reject if chi-square exceeds $\chi^2_{n-1,\alpha}$. Left-tailed: reject if it falls below $\chi^2_{n-1,1-\alpha}$. Two-tailed: use both ends with α/2 each.

Symbols: s^2 is the sample variance (divisor n - 1) and σ0^2 is the variance claimed in H0. Requires normal data.
cards.intuition_full: From the chi-square card, (n - 1) S^2 / σ^2 follows chi-square with n - 1 degrees of freedom when the data are normal. Under H0 we know σ^2 = σ0^2, so we can compute this quantity from the sample and compare it with a known distribution. Its mean is n - 1. If s^2 is about σ0^2, the statistic is near n - 1, as in the middle of the distribution. If s^2 is much larger than σ0^2, the statistic lands in the far right tail. The chi-square curve is not symmetric, so lower and upper critical values are different numbers, and you must read the correct tail from the table. This test is sensitive to non-normality, more than the test for a mean.

Statistic: chi-square = (n - 1) s^2 / σ0^2.
Degrees of freedom = n - 1 = 15, critical value 24.996.
30 > 24.996, so reject H0: the variance is larger than 9.

cards.title: Confidence interval duality
cards.simple: Imagine you computed a 95% range for the true average from your data, say 30 to 40. Now someone asks: would you reject the claim that the true average is 45? 45 is outside your range, so it is not a believable value, so yes, reject. What about the claim 35? That is inside your range, so it stays believable, so keep. In other words, the range is exactly the list of claims that the test would not reject. A 95% range and a 5% test are two views of the same thing. In exam words: a (1 - α) confidence interval contains exactly the values μ0 that a two-sided α test keeps.
cards.idea: A **(1 - α) confidence interval** is exactly the set of values μ0 that a two-sided α-level test would **not reject**. So you can run a test by looking at whether μ0 is inside the interval. Inside means fail to reject. Outside means reject.
cards.definition:
$$\mu_0\in\left(\bar x-z_{\alpha/2}\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n},\ \bar x+z_{\alpha/2}\tfrac{\sigma}{\sqrt n}\right)\iff |z|=\left|\frac{\bar x-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt n}\right|<z_{\alpha/2}$$

The two conditions are the same inequality rearranged. So a two-sided α test rejects H0: μ = μ0 exactly when μ0 is outside the (1 - α) interval.

The duality is for **two-sided** tests, and the level must match: 95% interval with 5% test.
cards.intuition_full: The test keeps μ0 when |x-bar - μ0| is less than z times the standard error. The interval collects the μ0 values for which that gap is small enough, which is x-bar plus or minus z times the standard error. They are the same inequality read in two ways: one starts from a fixed μ0 and checks x-bar, the other starts from the observed x-bar and lists all μ0 that pass. So a value at the edge of the interval has p-value exactly α. A narrower interval, such as 90%, matches a 10% test, which rejects more easily. Consequently a μ0 can be inside the 95% interval and outside the 90% interval, kept at 5% but rejected at 10%.

example.setup: A 95% confidence interval for μ is (30, 40). Using it, decide the two-sided 5% test for H0: μ = 45, H0: μ = 35 and H0: μ = 40.
steps: The interval (30, 40) is the set of μ0 values the two-sided 5% test keeps.
H0: μ = 45 lies outside the interval, so reject H0 at 5%.
H0: μ = 35 lies inside the interval, so fail to reject H0.
H0: μ = 40 is exactly on the edge: the p-value is exactly 0.05, so the decision is borderline.
The interval's centre is x-bar = 35 and its half-width is 5. For μ0 = 45, the gap is 10, which is twice the half-width.

examples.setup: Sample: n = 36, σ = 15, x-bar = 14.5, so SE = 2.5. A two-sided test of H0: μ = 20 is run at 5% and at 1%. Compare with the 95% and 99% intervals.
